extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science and biology; readers interested in conceptual foundations and origin-of-life hypotheses
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying conceptual and empirical criteria used to distinguish living from lifeless phenomena and to evaluate hypotheses about the origin of life (perpetuity, spontaneous generation, special creation).

rubrics_metrics.name: No single sense-impression defines life
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single sense-impression which can be said to be that of life; we lack perception of consciousness except in our own case and cannot infer consciousness for all life-forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to identify life by a single perceptual mark; definitions must be based on collections or sequences of sense-impressions and conceptual descriptions rather than one immediate impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is inadequate as a defining criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness cannot be used as the sole test of life: humans asleep or paralysed are still 'living', and low organisms respond to environment without evidence of stored sense-impressions that constitute consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid classifying organisms as living or lifeless solely on presence/absence of consciousness or hesitation between impression and exertion; the threshold of consciousness in the scale of life is indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical placeholders without phenomenal correlates (metakinesis, supermateriality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'metakinesis' (Lloyd Morgan) or 'supermateriality' are metaphysical names for putative intermediate states with no corresponding sense-impressions; they add imperceptible entities to explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not postulate imperceptible 'beings' or 'essences' unless they correspond to observable phenomena; prefer conceptual descriptions grounded in sense-impressions rather than metaphysical constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism as conceptual description vs ontological claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanism should be understood as a conceptual mode of describing sequences of sense-impressions (motions of corpuscles) rather than necessarily asserting a substratum of imperceptible moving parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicists/biologists should clarify whether 'mechanism' is being used as a conceptual shorthand. Avoid enticing biological explanations into metaphysical commitments by treating mechanism purely as ontological fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of physical laws to life (laws of motion criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To say life is mechanical requires determining whether the motions by which we conceptualise organic phenomena can be resumed in the same laws as inorganic phenomena; current knowledge does not settle whether laws for organic corpuscles are deducible from atomic laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether conservation laws or principles like inertia apply across the range of corpuscles invoked for living systems; be cautious—some general laws (e.g., conservation of energy) are not contradicted by life, but detailed reducibility remains unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary characteristics to define life (chemical, structural, dynamic, environmental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because primary, single-feature definitions fail, life must be defined by secondary characteristics: complex atomic structure based on compounds of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen (protoplasm/protein + water); characteristic modes of growth (inner growth vs crystal accretion); cyclical reproduction/division; and specific environmental requirements (moisture, temperature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a composite list of observable features to demarcate organic from inorganic; these characteristics 'suffice to mark off the organic from the inorganic' and form a rigid practical distinction in current experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use observational transitions (omne vivum e vivo) with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom 'omne vivum e vivo' (life from life) is closely associated with observed facts: transitions from living to lifeless are common, while the reverse has not been observed in ordinary experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer spontaneous generation merely because living things can become lifeless; reversibility of sequences of sense-impressions should not be assumed — physicists point to irreversible processes (e.g., degradation of energy) that undermine naive reversal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuity of life (biogenesis) hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis (a): life might be based on an immortal organic corpuscle that, with suitable environment, persists forever (perpetuity of life / biogenesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a conceptual model; it conflicts with geological/physical evidence for an azoic earth and requires strong inferences (e.g., primordial life capable of surviving unlike conditions). It is less adequate than hypotheses that bring both living and lifeless phenomena under a single formula without heavy inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneous generation (abiogenesis) hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis (b): life may be generated from special unions of inorganic corpuscles under favourable conditions (spontaneous generation / abiogenesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula unifies living and lifeless experiences without invoking unlike past conditions and is scientifically preferable in conceptual economy, but experimental reproduction may be impossible because the process could be irreversible and require enormously long periods and complex historical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special creation (ultra-scientific cause) hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis (c): life arose from the operation in time of some 'ultra-scientific' cause (special creation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered metaphysical rather than scientific here: it does not serve as a conceptual model that knits sense-impressions together or economises thought. Science should reject such hypotheses as not contributing to knowledge because they cannot be cross-examined or integrated into the explanatory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity criterion: hypotheses must integrate into conceptual models and economise thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific hypothesis must enable the classification and concise description of perceptual experience by forming conceptual links across phenomena; hypotheses that merely invoke unknown causes do not fulfil this role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating origin or classificatory hypotheses prefer those that bring unity to phenomena, permit conceptual shorthand, and follow from laws that describe present perceptual experience in the same field (theory of evolution preferred over special creation for scientific purposes).
